pages.c02-p01: Describe how a number is converted to a binary pattern for storage in a computer
pages.c02-p02: Demonstrate understanding of the following units of data: bit; nibble; byte; kilobyte; megabyte; gigabyte; and terabyte
pages.c02-p03: Demonstrate understanding of the following types of character representation: ASCII (7-bit and 8-bit); and Unicode
pages.c02-p04: Demonstrate understanding of and use number representation and convert between denary, binary and hexadecimal
pages.c02-p05: Demonstrate understanding of and use number representation and convert between denary, binary and hexadecimal
pages.c02-p06: Demonstrate understanding of and use number representation and convert between denary, binary and hexadecimal
pages.c02-p07: Perform the addition of two bytes and explain the meaning of overflow
pages.c02-p08: Describe and use appropriately the following data types: numeric (integer and real), date/time, character and string
pages.c02-p09: Demonstrate understanding of and use Boolean operators (AND, OR and NOT) and truth tables

q.q: Why do computers store all data in binary?
o: Binary numbers take up fewer digits than the same numbers in denary
Binary is easier for people to read and check than denary
Their circuits are made of transistors that are either on or off, giving only two states
Only binary can be translated into machine code by a compiler
q.why: Transistors have two states, on (1) and off (0). Binary needs more digits than denary, not fewer.

q.q: What is a bit?
o: A group of four binary digits
A group of eight binary digits
One hexadecimal digit
A single binary digit, 0 or 1
q.why: Bit is short for binary digit. Four bits is a nibble; eight is a byte.

q.q: In denary, each column is worth ten times the column to its right. How does this compare with binary?
o: In binary each column is worth ten times the column to its right
In binary each column is worth twice the column to its right
In binary each column is worth half the column to its right
In binary each column is worth sixteen times the column to its right
q.why: Binary is base 2, so place values double: 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on.

q.q: What are the place values of an 8-bit binary number, from left to right?
q.why: The rightmost bit is 1 (2⁰) and the leftmost of eight is 128 (2⁷).

q.q: Which 8-bit pattern stores the denary number 54?
How many different patterns can 5 bits make?
q.why: n bits give 2ⁿ patterns: 2⁵ = 32. 31 is the largest value, not the number of patterns.

q.q: What is the largest whole number that can be stored in one byte?
q.why: 11111111 = 255. There are 256 patterns, but one is used for 0.

q.q: A byte can hold 256 different values. Why is the largest value 255 and not 256?
o: The leftmost bit is always kept for the sign
One pattern is reserved to mark the end of the byte
One of the 256 patterns is used to store 0
256 needs a ninth bit for the carry, which is always lost
q.why: The values run 0 to 255, which is 256 values including 0.

q.q: How many different patterns can 16 bits make?
q.why: 2¹⁶ = 65 536 patterns, giving the range 0 to 65 535.

q.q: What range of whole numbers can a nibble (4 bits) store?
o: 0 to 16
0 to 15
1 to 16
0 to 7
q.why: 2⁴ = 16 patterns, so 0 to 15.

q.q: How many bits are in a nibble?
q.why: A nibble is half a byte: 4 bits.

q.q: Using the CCEA convention, how many bytes are in a kilobyte?
o: 1024 bits
q.why: CCEA mark schemes use 1024 bytes in a KB. Drive manufacturers sometimes use 1000.

q.q: Which list of units is in order from smallest to largest?
o: Bit, byte, nibble, kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte
Byte, kilobyte, gigabyte, megabyte, terabyte, nibble
Bit, nibble, byte, megabyte, kilobyte, terabyte
Nibble, byte, kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte
q.why: The ladder is bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB.

q.q: How many MB are in 3 GB?
q.why: Going to a smaller unit, multiply by 1024: 3 × 1024 = 3072 MB.

q.q: To convert kilobytes into megabytes, what should you do?
o: Multiply by 1024
Divide by 1024
Divide by 8
Multiply by 8
q.why: Going to a bigger unit, divide by 1024.

q.q: A file is 2048 KB. How big is it in MB?
o: 256 MB
2 MB
20 MB

q.q: How many bytes are 64 bits?
q.why: Bits to bytes: divide by 8, so 64 ÷ 8 = 8 bytes.

q.q: An external hard drive holds 4 TB. How many GB is that?
o: 4 GB
q.why: TB to GB is going to a smaller unit, so 4 × 1024 = 4096 GB.

q.q: Which is the largest amount of data?
o: 1 GB
900 MB
8000 bits
q.why: 1 GB = 1024 MB, which is more than 900 MB. 1000 KB is under 1 MB and 8000 bits is 1000 bytes.

q.q: Which item would typically be measured in megabytes?
o: A single ASCII character
A photo or an MP3 song
A short text document
An external hard drive
q.why: The notes give a photo or MP3 as a typical megabyte. A short text document is about a kilobyte.

q.q: A pupil has 300 photos, each 4 MB, and a 2 GB memory stick. Will they fit?
o: No: 300 × 4 = 1200 MB, which is more than 2 GB
Yes: 300 × 4 = 1200 MB, which is less than 2048 MB
Yes: 1200 MB is exactly 1.2 GB, which is less than 2 GB
No: 2 GB is only 2000 MB, so there is not enough room
q.why: Convert to the same unit: 2 GB = 2 × 1024 = 2048 MB, and 1200 MB fits. 1200 MB is about 1.17 GB, not exactly 1.2 GB.

q.q: What is a character set?
o: The set of keys available on a particular keyboard
An agreed list of characters and the unique binary code for each one
A list of the fonts installed on a computer
The set of data types a programming language allows
q.why: A character set maps each character to a unique code.

q.q: What does ASCII stand for?
o: American System Code for International Information
Advanced Standard Character for Information Interchange
American Standard Character Input Interface
American Standard Code for Information Interchange
q.why: ASCII is the American Standard Code for Information Interchange.

q.q: How many characters can 7-bit ASCII represent?
q.why: 2⁷ = 128 codes, numbered 0 to 127.

q.q: In ASCII, the code for 'A' is 65. What is the code for 'E'?
q.why: Letters are in order: A 65, B 66, C 67, D 68, E 69. 101 is lower-case 'e'.

q.q: In ASCII, the code for 'a' is 97. What is the code for 'g'?
Why can text be sorted into alphabetical order by comparing ASCII codes?
o: ASCII codes are stored in hexadecimal, which sorts automatically
Each character takes exactly one byte, so they line up
ASCII codes 0 to 31 are control codes that tell the computer how to sort
The letter codes are in order, so A (65) comes before B (66) and so on
q.why: Because the codes run in order, comparing codes compares letters.

q.q: Why was 8-bit ASCII not enough for Chinese or Japanese text?
o: It used only 7 bits, so it could not store any accented letters
Its codes were stored in hexadecimal, which those languages do not use
Its 256 codes could never hold languages with thousands of characters
It stored each character in four bytes, which wasted too much space
q.why: Those languages have thousands of characters, far more than 256 codes.

q.q: In Unicode, what is a code point?
o: The unique number given to each character
The number of bits used to store each character
The place in a file where a character is stored
A control code that marks the end of a line
q.why: Unicode gives every character its own number, called a code point.

q.q: Why can plain ASCII text still be read correctly using Unicode?
o: Unicode's first 128 code points are the same as ASCII
Unicode converts all ASCII text into hexadecimal first
Unicode stores every ASCII character in 32 bits
Unicode ignores any character with a code below 128
q.why: ASCII is a subset of Unicode because the first 128 codes match.

q.q: Which Unicode encoding stores ASCII characters in one byte, making it backward compatible, and is the most common on the web?
o: UTF-8
UTF-16
UTF-32
Extended ASCII
q.why: UTF-8 is variable length (8 to 32 bits) and uses one byte for ASCII characters.

q.q: Which Unicode encoding uses 32 bits for every character?
o: UTF-32
UTF-16
UTF-8
8-bit ASCII
q.why: UTF-32 is fixed length: simple but wasteful, four times the storage of ASCII for English.

q.q: Which is a genuine disadvantage of Unicode compared with ASCII?
o: It covers fewer languages, so many characters cannot be shown
It can need more bits per character, so files can be larger
It cannot represent the English alphabet
Its first 128 codes are different from ASCII, so old files break
q.why: Unicode can need more storage per character. It covers far more languages, and its first 128 codes match ASCII.

q.q: A pupil is asked for two differences between ASCII and Unicode and writes: "ASCII has fewer characters. Unicode has more characters." How many marks would this likely gain?
o: One, because it is the same difference written twice the other way round
Two, because two separate statements have been made
None, because ASCII and Unicode have the same number of characters
Two, because both statements are factually correct
q.why: Give two different points, such as range of characters and bits per character.

q.q: What is 47 as an 8-bit binary number?
q.why: 32 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 47. 11110100 is the same bits written backwards.

q.q: What is 01010000 in denary?
q.why: Add the place values under each 1: 64 + 16 = 80.

q.q: What is 200 as an 8-bit binary number?
What is 10101010 in denary?
What is 00011111 in denary?
What is 10110101 in denary?
What is 99 as an 8-bit binary number?
Using the division method, 25 gives the remainders 1, 0, 0, 1, 1 in the order they were worked out. What is 25 in 8-bit binary?
q.why: Read the remainders from the bottom up: 11001, padded to 00011001.

q.q: In the division method of converting denary to binary, which remainder gives the rightmost bit?
o: The first remainder worked out
The last remainder worked out
The largest remainder
The middle remainder
q.why: The first remainder is the 1s column; reading from the top gives the bits backwards.

q.q: A question asks for 6 as a one-byte binary number. Which answer is best?
q.why: An 8-bit answer should include the leading zeros. 01100000 has the bits in the wrong columns.

q.q: In the subtraction method, what do you do at each column, working from the left?
o: Divide the number by the place value and write the remainder as the bit
Write 1 under every place value smaller than the number
If the place value fits into what is left, write 1 and subtract it; otherwise write 0
Add the place value to the number and write 1 if the total is even
q.why: Subtract the largest place value that fits, left to right, writing 1 or 0.

q.q: Hexadecimal is base 16. Which symbols does it use?
o: 0 to 9 and then A to G
0 to 9 and then A to F
0 to 15 written as two digits
1 to 9 and then A to G
q.why: Hex needs sixteen symbols: 0–9 then A (10) to F (15).

q.q: What is the hex digit for denary 13?
o: C
E
D
B

q.q: Why does one hex digit stand for exactly one nibble?
o: 16 = 2⁸, so one hex digit has the same values as a byte
Each hex digit is stored in 4 bytes of memory
Hex digits are always half the size of denary digits
16 = 2⁴, so one hex digit has the same 16 possible values as 4 bits
q.why: 4 bits give 16 patterns, the same as one hex digit, so a byte is two hex digits.

q.q: What is 01111011 in hexadecimal?
o: 7B
7D
B7
q.why: Split into nibbles: 0111 = 7 and 1011 = 11 = B.

q.q: What is the hex number C4 in binary?
What is 66 in hexadecimal?
o: 4A
q.why: 66 ÷ 16 = 4 remainder 2, so 42.

q.q: What is 200 in hexadecimal?
o: 8C
B8
C4
C8
q.why: 200 ÷ 16 = 12 remainder 8; 12 = C.

q.q: What is the hex number 3B in denary?
q.why: 3 × 16 + 11 = 59. 311 comes from writing 3 then 11 side by side.

q.q: What is the hex number FF in denary?
q.why: 15 × 16 + 15 = 255, the largest byte.

q.q: Which is a genuine advantage of hexadecimal over binary?
o: It takes up less storage space in memory
The processor executes hex faster than binary
It is shorter, so people can read and copy it with fewer errors
It lets the computer store negative numbers
q.why: Hex is for people; the computer still stores binary, so it saves no space.

q.q: Which is a common use of hexadecimal?
o: Storing each digit of a price for a petrol pump display
Storing negative numbers inside the processor
Colour codes in HTML and CSS, such as #1D6B53
Making stored files take up less storage space
q.why: Hex is used for colour codes, MAC addresses, memory addresses and error codes.

q.q: In the signed methods of storing numbers, what does a 1 in the most significant bit (MSB) show?
o: The number is positive
The number is odd
Overflow has occurred
The number is negative
q.why: In each signed method the MSB is 0 for positive and 1 for negative.

q.q: What is −45 in 8-bit sign and magnitude? (+45 is 00101101)
q.why: Sign and magnitude only sets the MSB to 1. 11010010 is one's complement and 11010011 is two's complement.

q.q: What is −45 in 8-bit one's complement? (+45 is 00101101)
q.why: One's complement inverts every bit of the positive number.

q.q: What is −45 in 8-bit two's complement? (+45 is 00101101)
q.why: Invert to 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011.

q.q: What is −20 in 8-bit two's complement? (+20 is 00010100)
q.why: Invert to 11101011 and add 1: 11101100. 11101011 is one's complement; 10010100 is sign and magnitude.

q.q: What range of numbers can 8-bit two's complement store?
q.why: The MSB is worth −128 and the other bits add to at most +127.

q.q: Why do real processors use two's complement rather than sign and magnitude?
o: There are two zeros, which makes it easier to check answers
There is only one zero and binary addition works directly, so subtraction can be done by adding
It is easier for people to read the size of the number
It can store larger positive numbers, up to +255
q.why: Sign and magnitude has two zeros and gives wrong answers when adding mixed signs.

q.q: In 8-bit two's complement, what is 10000000?
q.why: The MSB is worth −128 and all other bits are 0.

q.q: A pupil inverts every bit of a positive number to make it negative in two's complement, but the check does not match. What has gone wrong?
o: They should have changed only the MSB to 1
They should have added 1 before inverting the bits
They forgot to add 1; inverting alone gives one's complement
They should have inverted only the rightmost four bits
q.why: Two's complement is invert, then add 1.

q.q: How is 395 stored in binary coded decimal (BCD)?
q.why: Each denary digit gets its own nibble: 3 = 0011, 9 = 1001, 5 = 0101. 0001 1000 1011 is ordinary binary for 395.

q.q: How is 72 stored in BCD?
q.why: 7 = 0111 and 2 = 0010. 0100 1000 is ordinary binary for 72.

q.q: Why might a petrol pump display use binary coded decimal?
o: Each digit is stored separately, so it is easy to send to a digital display
BCD stores numbers in fewer bits than ordinary binary
BCD can store negative prices using the MSB
BCD uses the patterns 1010 to 1111 for the decimal point
q.why: BCD suits displays and avoids rounding errors in money, though it wastes some space.

q.q: What is 1 + 1 in binary addition?
o: 1 carry 1
0 carry 1
2 carry 0
1 carry 0
q.why: The column total is 2, so write 0 and carry 1.

q.q: What is overflow?
o: The result of a calculation is too large for the number of bits available, so the extra bit is lost
The result of a calculation is negative, so it cannot be stored in a byte
A carry is written into a column that already holds a 1
The program runs out of main memory while adding numbers
q.why: Overflow is a result too large for the bits available; the extra bit is lost and the stored answer is wrong.

q.q: Which 8-bit unsigned addition causes overflow?
q.why: 150 + 120 = 270, more than 255. The others total 200, 250 and 255.

q.q: Adding 200 + 100 in 8 bits gives 1 00101100. What value is stored in the byte?
q.why: The ninth bit is lost, leaving 00101100 = 32 + 8 + 4 = 44.

q.q: In unsigned 8-bit addition, how can you spot that overflow has happened?
o: The leftmost bit of the answer is a 1
There is a carry out of the leftmost (128) column
The answer has more 1s than 0s
There is a carry into the rightmost column
q.why: A carry out of the 128 column, or a total above 255, means overflow. A leftmost 1 just means 128 or more.

q.q: What is the effect of overflow on a program?
o: The stored result is incorrect, so the program may give wrong answers, behave unexpectedly or crash
The program automatically switches to a larger data type and carries on
The processor adds an extra bit to the byte to hold the answer
The program stops and displays the correct answer as a warning
q.why: The extra bit is lost, so the stored answer is wrong.

q.q: A C# int holds 2147483647 (int.MaxValue). What happens when 1 is added to it?
o: It becomes 2147483648 and is stored correctly
The program shows an overflow error and stops
It wraps round to the most negative int, with no error message
It stays at 2147483647 because that is the limit
q.why: The value wraps round silently, which is a logic error waiting to happen.

q.q: A program might need to store values larger than a C# int can hold. Which is the best way to avoid overflow?
o: Use a char, because characters take up more bits
Use a data type big enough for the values, such as long (64 bits)
Store the values in hexadecimal, which uses less space
Use BCD so that each digit is stored separately
q.why: Choose a type big enough (long) or check the range first. Hex saves no storage.

q.q: In 8-bit two's complement, how is overflow detected?
o: The carry into the leftmost column is different from the carry out of it
Any carry out of the leftmost column means overflow
The answer has a 1 as its most significant bit
The two numbers being added have different signs
q.why: With signed numbers a ninth carry bit alone is ignored; differing last two carries mean overflow.

q.q: Why does every variable in C# have a data type?
o: It tells the computer what kind of value is stored, how much memory to use and which operations are allowed
It tells the computer which line of the program the variable is declared on
It decides whether the program will be compiled or interpreted
It sets the starting value of the variable to zero
q.why: The data type decides memory and allowed operations, and makes validation possible.

q.q: Which data type should store a race time of 12.84 seconds?
o: Integer
Character
Real
String
q.why: It has a decimal part, so it is real.

q.q: Which data type is best for a mobile phone number such as 07700 900123?
o: Integer
Real
Character
String
q.why: It has a leading 0 and is never calculated with; a number type would lose the 0.

q.q: A variable records whether a pupil has paid for a trip. Which data type should it be?
o: String
Character
Boolean
Integer
q.why: There are only two states, paid or not, so Boolean.

q.q: Which data type is best for the number of tickets sold for a concert?
o: Real
String
Boolean
Integer
q.why: Counting whole things uses integer.

q.q: Which data type is best for storing a pupil's grade, such as 'A'?
o: String
Integer
Character
Boolean
q.why: A single grade or initial is one character.

q.q: What is the difference between a character and a string?
o: A character holds letters only; a string holds digits only
A character holds one symbol; a string holds a sequence of characters
A character holds a sequence of symbols; a string holds one symbol
A character holds whole numbers; a string holds text
q.why: char is one letter, digit or symbol; string is text.

q.q: Which is the best justification for storing the cost of a holiday as real?
o: Real, because the cost includes pence
Real, because it is a number
Real, because it is the most accurate data type
Real, because money is always a whole number of pounds
q.why: Justify by linking the type to the data: the cost has a fractional part.

q.q:
int nights = Convert.ToInt32(Console.ReadLine());
Why is Convert.ToInt32 needed here?
o: Console.ReadLine() returns a real number, which must be rounded to an integer
Without it the program would read only the first character typed
It checks that the value entered is within a sensible range
Console.ReadLine() always returns a string, which must be converted before arithmetic
q.why: Input arrives as a string, so it must be converted before calculating.
Casting marks to double keeps the decimal part. Without the cast, int / int would give 3.

q.q: In C#, what does new DateTime() with nothing in the brackets give?
o: 1 January in the year 1
Today's date
The current date and time
An error, because a date must be supplied
q.why: Use DateTime.Now or DateTime.Today for the current date; new DateTime() gives 1 January, year 1.

q.q: When is A AND B true?
o: When at least one of A and B is true
When exactly one of A and B is true
When both A and B are false
Only when both A and B are true
q.why: AND needs both inputs true.

q.q: When is A OR B true?
o: Only when both A and B are true
Only when exactly one of A and B is true
Only when both A and B are false
When at least one of A and B is true, including both
q.why: OR is true if either or both inputs are true. Exactly one is XOR.

q.q: What does NOT do to its input?
o: Leaves it the same unless the other input is true
Reverses it, so true becomes false and false becomes true
Makes the output false whatever the input
Combines it with a second input using AND
q.why: NOT has one input and reverses it.

q.q: How many rows does a truth table with 3 inputs need?
q.why: n inputs need 2ⁿ rows: 2³ = 8 rows.

q.q: How many rows does a truth table with 4 inputs need?
q.why: n inputs need 2ⁿ rows: 2⁴ = 16 rows.

q.q: If P = 1 and Q = 0, what is NOT (P OR Q)?
o: It depends on a third input
P OR Q is undefined when the inputs differ
q.why: P OR Q = 1, and NOT 1 = 0.

q.q: If P = 1 and Q = 1, what is NOT (P AND Q)?
q.why: P AND Q = 1, and NOT 1 = 0.

q.q: If A = 1, B = 0 and C = 1, what is (A OR B) AND NOT C?
o: It cannot be worked out without a truth table
q.why: A OR B = 1; NOT C = 0; 1 AND 0 = 0.

q.q: Which C# operator means OR?
q.why: || is OR, && is AND and ! is NOT. == compares values.

q.q: A loop should repeat until the user types Y or N: while (reply != "Y" ___ reply != "N"). Which operator goes in the gap?
q.why: It needs AND. With || the condition is always true, so the loop never ends.
